problem: VLN-CE agents rely on depth, odometry, maps or panoramic waypoint predictors. These inputs cause Sim2Real gaps (depth and colour domain shift, odometer noise) and generalize poorly to new scenes and instruction styles. Earlier LLM-based VLN agents work in discrete nav-graphs or record history as text descriptions, so they cannot output executable low-level actions from raw video.
motivation: Generalization, both to unseen scenes or datasets and from simulation to the real world, is the main obstacle to deploying VLN. The existing RGB-only low-level baselines essentially fail: RGB-CMA reaches 5% SR on R2R-CE. The authors observe that large video VLMs carry web-scale knowledge. They argue that a human-like formulation (monocular RGB video in, next action out) removes the sensor-induced domain gaps entirely.
key_idea: Fine-tune a video VLM (LLaMA-VID with Vicuna-7B) to read the whole monocular RGB video history plus the instruction. It emits the next low-level action in language, e.g. 'move forward 75 cm' or 'turn left 30 degrees'. Training co-mixes R2R-CE oracle and DAgger step samples, instruction-reasoning samples, and web video QA data.
insight: Representing history as compressed video tokens is far better than text or map summaries. In Table V, text-based history gets 0 SR, map+text 9.13, and ego-view+text 23.5, versus 37.4 for video on R2R-CE val-unseen, and the text pipeline is about 2x slower. Co-training with web video QA data is the single most important ingredient: removing it drops SR from 37.4 to 24.7. Instruction-reasoning samples (to 31.1 without them) and DAgger non-oracle samples (to 34.2 without them) also help. The output formulation matters: asking the VLM to regress continuous waypoints (location and orientation) collapses to 0 SR. Also, 4 grid-pooled tokens per history frame is the sweet spot: 1 token gives 23.9 SR, while 16 tokens give 38.0 SR at about 2.2x the latency.
method: Backbone: LLaMA-VID architecture. EVA-CLIP vision encoder (256 patches/frame), a Q-Former query generator with a BERT text encoder, two cross-modal projectors, and a Vicuna-7B LLM.

Per-frame observation tokens: one instruction-queried token, formed by Q-Former instruction-aware queries cross-attending to the frame's patch features and then average-pooled and projected. Plus instruction-agnostic tokens from grid average-pooling of the EVA-CLIP feature map: 64 tokens for the current frame, 4 (2x2 grid) for each historical frame.
Special-token prompt format: <HIS>{history frames}</HIS><OBS>{current frame}</OBS><NAV>{instruction}. This separates history, current view and task, and the LLM answers with the next action.

Language action output: an action type in {FORWARD, TURN-LEFT, TURN-RIGHT, STOP} with a quantitative argument (distance or degrees). It is parsed by regular expressions, giving 100% valid actions on R2R-CE val-unseen, and executed step by step without depth, odometry or maps.

Hybrid navigation data: 320k step-wise oracle samples from R2R-CE train (61 MP3D scenes). Plus 180k DAgger-style non-oracle samples collected by rolling out the oracle-trained model in VLN-CE, for 510k action samples in total.

Co-training with auxiliary tasks: 10k instruction-reasoning samples (trajectory video → instruction) and 763k web video QA/caption data from LLaMA-VID for anti-forgetting. Trained for 1 epoch, updating only the LLM and text encoder, on 24 A100s for about 28 h.
Deployment: the model runs on a remote A100 server receiving compressed RGB frames from a Turtlebot4 (Azure Kinect RGB only). It takes about 1.2–1.5 s per action.

results: On R2R-CE val-unseen, NaVid gets SR 37.4 / SPL 35.9 / NE 5.47 using only monocular RGB. RGB-only baselines score far lower (RGB-CMA 5.00 / 4.43). The best low-level RGB-D+odometry method, WS-MGMap, has a higher SR (38.9) but a lower SPL (34.3), so the 'SOTA' claim holds for SPL/NE/OS, not SR. NaVid remains well below panoramic waypoint methods such as ETPNav (57 SR). In cross-dataset R2R→RxR-CE it reaches SR 23.8 / SPL 21.2, versus A2Nav 16.8 / 6.3 and WS-MGMap 15.0 / 12.1. In the real world (4 scenes, 200 instructions) it reaches 76–92% SR on simple and 40–56% on complex instructions, far above WS-MGMap (44–60% / 12–32%) and Seq2Seq/CMA (≈0%).
limitations: High latency: about 1.2–1.5 s per action on a remote A100, with the 7B VLM queried at every step; each extra history token increases cost further.

Long-horizon instructions can suffer from long-context token growth, and the lack of long-video annotation data makes this worse. Adding DAgger data on the R2R train scenes gives only marginal gains because of limited scene and instruction diversity.

Absolute SR on R2R-CE (37.4) is still far below panoramic/waypoint-based methods and slightly below WS-MGMap. The real-world evaluation uses the authors' own simple/complex instruction sets, and the model runs off-board.
